newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian coffee trade ignores diving London robustas.
newsitem.headline: Asian coffee trade ignores diving London robustas.

text.p: Asian coffee exporters are ignoring what they feel are "ridiculously" low prices after London robustas dived almost 10 percent overnight, traders said on Wednesday.
London robusta futures tumbled on Tuesday, with the benchmark September contract plunging US$170 to a session low of $1,565 a tonne before closing $150 down on the day at $1,585.
"London is at a ridiculously low level. The exporters don't look at London any more. What London is doing is not relevant to the trade here at the moment," a dealer for a coffee house said.
"The futures market has collapsed, but the origins will not be following this market lower," a senior trader added.
Traders said coffee supplies were tight in Asia and exporters would opt to sell at levels they want rather than take large losses as a result of falling coffee prices.
Indonesia's key Grade 4 coffee, 80 defects, was quoted by the trade at around $50-$100 over basis September robustas in London although one dealer quoted Grade 4 at $50 under the September contract.
The dealers said trade houses already short on coffee would have no choice but to pay the price the exporters are asking.
"Coffee is very scarce. In Thailand, Vietnam and Laos, there is no more coffee. People who need the coffee will pay the price the exporters want," a trader predicted.
Asian coffee traders expected the London market to bounce back later on Wednesday after yesterday's meltdown.
"It seems logical that there should be a bounce although we can go down to $1,500 or even $1,400. But this has been all funds. It has nothing to do with the coffee trade," said one.
"It should be $40 higher. We should see a bounce," another dealer said.
But one trader said there may be follow through selling in the market and forecast London robustas wuold be "$50 down. It's a good guessing game right now where the whole thing is headed."
The coffee business in the region, however, will probably remain quiet with most of the U.S. and European roasters away on summer holidays.
"The roasters tend to go to sleep during this time of the year. A lot of them are also enjoying a break. The coffee trade is pretty quiet," one coffee analyst added.
Dealers predict coffee trading would pick up steam beginning from next month when roasters buy their winter supplies.

"They will start picking up their winter roasting supplies towards the end of August so business should pick up by then. For now, nothing is moving. I think the funds came in and sold off their positions in New York and London before taking off for their own holidays," one said.
The robusta coffee contract in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) was untraded on Tuesday and it was likewise untraded on Monday.
The July robusta contract was indicated on Tuesday $90 lower at $1,506 a tonne. The September contract was also indicated $90 down at $1,499.
